text:
The animal known for its long neck is the giraffe.

Jim stood in the center of the advanced yoga studio, a man who had clearly confused "advanced" with "adventurous." He was attempting to hold a variation of the Standing Split, a pose that required balance, flexibility, and inner peace. Jim possessed none of these, but he did possess a digestive system that had recently decided to wage war on his dignity.

As the instructor, a serene woman named Serenity, whispered, "Find your center, breathe into the void," Jim found his center to be a tight knot of anxiety and gas. He wobbled. His left leg trembled like a leaf in a hurricane. To compensate, he clenched every muscle in his body, including the ones he didn’t know he had.

The first sound was a low, mournful groan, like a cello string snapping. Then, as he shifted his weight to correct his posture, a sharp, high-pitched *toot* escaped him, echoing off the mirrored walls.

Serenity didn’t flinch. "Let the sound be part of your breath," she said calmly.

Jim, sweating profusely, tried to ignore the humiliation. He pushed harder into the pose, his face turning a shade of purple that matched the yoga blocks. He held his breath, holding it so tightly that his eyes bulged. The pressure built. He was a human balloon animal waiting to pop.

He tried to exhale slowly, as instructed. Instead, he released a sound that was less of a breath and more of a tuba being dropped down a flight of stairs. It was a long, resonant, undulating noise that seemed to vibrate in the chest of everyone in the room.

The class, previously a picture of zen, cracked. A woman in the back snorted. A man in the front choked on his own saliva. Serenity’s eye twitched, just once.

Jim, unaware of the chaos he was causing, thought the silence was judgment. He thought he needed to push harder. He leaned forward, trying to deepen the stretch. This was his fatal mistake. The combination of the deep abdominal compression and the awkward angle created a perfect storm.

*PFFFFFFFFRRRRRT.*

It wasn’t just a noise; it was a performance. It lasted for a full three seconds, rising in pitch and volume before trailing off into a squeak.

The silence that followed was heavier than the yoga
